summary: C file I/O is built on the `FILE *` stream abstraction from `<stdio.h>`. A stream wraps an operating-system file descriptor with a buffer, a position and error flags, and gives you text and binary read and write functions. It matters because every tool, server, database and parser reads or writes files, and the subtle parts (buffering, modes, return values, partial reads, `fseek`) are where real bugs and interview questions live.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A C program talks to files through streams. `fopen` returns a `FILE *` that you pass to `fprintf`, `fgets`, `fread`, `fwrite`, `fseek` and finally `fclose`. Three streams are already open when `main` starts: `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr`. Underneath, each stream owns a file descriptor (on POSIX systems) and an in-memory buffer, so most calls never touch the kernel. This lesson covers opening modes, text and binary I/O, positioning, buffering, error handling and the lower-level POSIX descriptor API.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Stream**: a sequence of bytes accessed through a `FILE *`. The `FILE` structure is opaque. Never copy it and never touch its fields.

**Text mode versus binary mode**: in text mode the library may translate line endings (`\r\n` to `\n` on Windows). On Linux and macOS the two are identical, but write `"b"` anyway for portable binary code.

**Mode string**: `"r"` read (file must exist), `"w"` write (create or truncate), `"a"` append (create, always write at the end), plus `"+"` for update, for example `"r+"`, `"w+"`, `"a+"`. C11 adds `"x"` (with `w`) to fail if the file already exists.
**File position indicator**: the offset of the next byte to read or write. `fseek`, `ftell`, `rewind`, `fgetpos` and `fsetpos` move or report it.
**Buffering**: fully buffered (files), line buffered (terminals) or unbuffered (`stderr`). `fflush` pushes buffered output to the OS.
**EOF and error indicators**: two separate flags per stream. `feof(fp)` and `ferror(fp)` query them, `clearerr(fp)` resets both.
**`EOF` constant**: a negative `int` (usually -1) returned by `fgetc`, `getchar` and friends. It is why those functions return `int`, not `char`.
**File descriptor**: the small integer the kernel uses (0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr). `fileno(fp)` gets it from a stream, `fdopen(fd, mode)` builds a stream from one.
**`errno`**: set by failing library calls. `perror("msg")` and `strerror(errno)` turn it into text.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: The usual life cycle is open, check, use, check, close. `fopen` asks the OS to open the path, allocates a `FILE` with a buffer (often 4096 or 8192 bytes), and returns a pointer or `NULL`. Writes copy bytes into the buffer and only call `write(2)` when the buffer fills, when you call `fflush` or `fclose`, or when the program exits normally. Reads work in reverse: the first read pulls a whole block into the buffer and later reads are served from memory.

Notice three habits. Every `fopen` is checked for `NULL`. The `fscanf` loop tests the return value (the count of items converted) instead of testing `feof` first. The `%31s` width keeps a long word from overflowing the 32-byte buffer. Even `fclose` is checked, because on a buffered write stream the final flush happens there and a full disk shows up only at that moment.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Formatted I/O**: `fprintf` and `fscanf` convert between text and values. Easy to read, slow, and `fscanf` is fragile on bad input.
**Character I/O**: `fgetc`, `fputc`, `getc`, `putc`, `ungetc` (one guaranteed pushback). Good for tokenizers.
**Line I/O**: `fgets(buf, n, fp)` reads up to `n-1` characters and keeps the newline. `fputs` writes a string without adding one. Avoid `gets`; it was removed in C11.

**Block (binary) I/O**: `fread(ptr, size, count, fp)` and `fwrite(...)` move raw bytes and return the number of items transferred. Use for structs and images, but remember padding and endianness make the file non-portable.
**Positioning**: `fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET | SEEK_CUR | SEEK_END)`, `ftell`, `rewind`. For files over 2 GiB on 32-bit `long` platforms use `fseeko`/`ftello` (POSIX) or `_fseeki64`.
**Whole-file helpers**: `remove`, `rename`, `tmpfile`, `tmpnam` (unsafe), `mkstemp` (POSIX, preferred).
**POSIX descriptors**: `open`, `read`, `write`, `lseek`, `close`, `fsync`. No library buffering, exact control, used for sockets, pipes and durability.
**Memory-mapped files**: `mmap` maps a file into the address space so you access it as an array. Best for large random access.
**`fmemopen` and `open_memstream`** (POSIX 2008): treat a memory buffer as a `FILE *`, which makes functions that take streams testable without touching disk.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: A buffered `fgetc` or `fputc` costs a few nanoseconds because it only moves one byte inside the buffer. An unbuffered `write(1, &c, 1)` per byte costs a system call, about 100 to 1000 ns each, so a megabyte written byte by byte is hundreds of milliseconds.
Default buffer size is `BUFSIZ`, at least 256 and 8192 on glibc. `setvbuf(fp, NULL, _IOFBF, 1 << 16)` before the first I/O gives a 64 KiB buffer for bulk transfers.
`fread` of one 4096-byte block is far cheaper than 4096 calls of `fgetc`. Prefer block reads and parse in memory.

`fseek` on a read stream discards the buffer, so seeking back and forth by small amounts wastes reads. Sequential access is the cheapest pattern; random access costs about one block read per seek on a miss.
`fflush` moves data to the kernel page cache only. `fsync(fileno(fp))` forces it to disk and can take milliseconds on spinning drives and still around 0.1 to 1 ms on SSDs.
`ftell` gives a `long`, which is 32 bits on 64-bit Windows and so caps at about 2 GiB. `fgetpos` and `fsetpos` avoid that limit.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Not checking `fopen`**: a `NULL` `FILE *` passed to `fprintf` is undefined behavior and usually a crash.
**`while (!feof(fp))`**: `feof` becomes true only after a read has already hit the end, so the loop runs once too often and processes garbage. Test the read function's return value.
**Storing `fgetc` in a `char`**: on platforms where `char` is unsigned `EOF` is never seen, and where it is signed a valid byte `0xFF` looks like `EOF`. Use `int`.
**Using `"w"` by mistake**: it truncates the file at open time, before your first write. Use `"a"` to add and `"r+"` to edit in place.
**Mixing reads and writes** on an update stream without an intervening `fflush` or `fseek` is undefined behavior.
**`fgets` and the newline**: the trailing `\n` is kept. Strip it with `buf[strcspn(buf, "\n")] = 0`. A line longer than the buffer comes back in pieces.
**`fscanf("%s")` without a width** is as dangerous as `gets` and overflows the buffer on long input.
**Forgetting `fclose`**: leaks the descriptor (typical limit 1024 per process by default) and may lose buffered data if the program is killed.
**Writing structs with `fwrite`**: padding bytes, pointer members and byte order make the file unreadable on another machine or compiler. Serialize field by field for portable formats.
**Reading a text file in binary mode on Windows** leaves `\r` before every `\n`.
**Closing a stream twice** or using it after `fclose` is undefined behavior, a cousin of use-after-free.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Config and log files**: `fopen(path, "a")` plus line-buffered writes. Servers often open logs with `O_APPEND` so concurrent writers do not overwrite one another.
**Parsers and interpreters**: read the source with `fread` into one buffer, then parse in memory.
**Databases and key-value stores**: use raw descriptors, `pwrite`, `fsync` and write-ahead logs to guarantee data survives a crash.
**Unix filters**: programs like `cat`, `grep`, `sort` read `stdin` and write `stdout`, so shell pipes and redirection compose them.

**Atomic updates**: write to a temporary file in the same directory, `fsync`, then `rename` over the original. `rename` is atomic on POSIX, so readers see the old or the new file, never a half-written one.
**Binary formats**: image headers, ELF files and network captures are read with `fread` into structs or byte arrays, with explicit endianness conversion.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **What does `fopen` return on failure?** `NULL`, with `errno` set. Check it every time.
**Difference between `"w"` and `"a"`?** `"w"` truncates an existing file. `"a"` keeps content and always writes at the end regardless of `fseek`.
**Why does `fgetc` return `int`?** To hold all 256 byte values plus a distinct `EOF`.
**Why is `while(!feof(fp))` wrong?** The flag is set only after a failed read, so you process one extra bogus iteration.
**`fread` returned less than requested; what now?** Either EOF or an error. Call `feof` and `ferror` to tell which.
**`FILE *` versus file descriptor?** `FILE *` is buffered, portable ISO C. A descriptor is a POSIX integer for unbuffered kernel calls.
**How do you get the size of a file?** `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END)` then `ftell`, or `fstat`/`stat` on POSIX, which is cheaper and works for large files.

subtopics.title: Opening, creating and closing
subtopics.summary: `fopen` modes decide whether a file is created, truncated or appended.

sections.body: A file is created by opening it with `"w"`, `"a"` (or their `+` forms). Opening with `"r"` or `"r+"` fails if it does not exist. `"w"` destroys old content immediately, so open the new file under a temporary name when you cannot afford to lose the old one. `fclose` flushes buffered output and releases the descriptor. Its return value is 0 on success and `EOF` on error, and it is the place where a deferred write error such as a full disk first appears.

subtopics.title: Reading text: fgets, fscanf and getline
subtopics.summary: Pick the reader that cannot overflow and reports the end of input correctly.

sections.body: `fgets` is the safe default for line input. `fscanf` is fine for simple, trusted formats when you check its return value and bound every `%s`. POSIX `getline` allocates and grows a buffer for you, so it handles lines of any length, but you must `free` the buffer.

Reading is complete when the loop's read call fails. Afterwards distinguish normal end from failure: `feof(fp)` true means you consumed everything, `ferror(fp)` true means the OS reported an I/O problem.

subtopics.title: Binary I/O with fread and fwrite
subtopics.summary: Move raw bytes in blocks and always check the item count.

sections.body: `fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp)` returns the number of complete items written, which should equal the count you asked for. Reading mirrors it. Put the element size in the second argument and the count in the third so a short transfer reports whole items.

This file is tied to one compiler and architecture. `sizeof(Rec)` includes 4 padding bytes between `id` and `score` on typical 64-bit ABIs, and integers are stored in host byte order. For files that must move between machines, write each field with a fixed width (`uint32_t`) and a fixed byte order, or use a text or schema-based format.

subtopics.title: Moving the file pointer
subtopics.summary: fseek, ftell and rewind give random access for seekable files.

sections.body: `fseek(fp, off, whence)` takes `SEEK_SET` (from the start), `SEEK_CUR` (relative) or `SEEK_END` (from the end). Returns 0 on success. In text mode only offsets returned by `ftell` (or 0) are guaranteed meaningful. Pipes and terminals are not seekable, so `fseek` fails with `ESPIPE`.

subtopics.title: Buffering, flushing and durability
subtopics.summary: Know which layer your bytes are in: user buffer, kernel cache, or disk.

sections.body: Three layers sit between `fprintf` and the platter. The stdio buffer lives in your process. `fflush` hands it to the kernel, which keeps it in the page cache. `fsync` asks the kernel to commit to the device. A crash of your process after `fflush` loses nothing, a power failure before `fsync` can lose everything. `setvbuf` changes the mode: `_IOFBF` full, `_IOLBF` line, `_IONBF` none, and must be called before any other operation on the stream.
sections.code:
setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0);      /* line buffer even when piped */
fprintf(log, "event %d\n", id);
fflush(log);                            /* to the kernel */
fsync(fileno(log));                     /* to the disk (POSIX, <unistd.h>) */

sections.body: A common surprise: `printf("loading...")` without a newline may not appear before a long computation because the terminal is line buffered. Call `fflush(stdout)`, or write progress to `stderr`, which is unbuffered.

subtopics.title: Standard streams and redirection
subtopics.summary: stdin, stdout and stderr are ordinary FILE pointers that the shell can rewire.

sections.body: Streams 0, 1 and 2 are inherited from the parent process. `prog < in.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt` makes the shell open files and install them as descriptors 0, 1 and 2 before your `main` runs, so `scanf` and `printf` need no change. `freopen(path, mode, stdout)` does the same inside the program. Keep normal output on `stdout` and diagnostics on `stderr` so users can separate them, and use the exit status (`EXIT_SUCCESS` or `EXIT_FAILURE`) to report errors to scripts.

subtopics.title: Error handling patterns
subtopics.summary: Check every call, report with errno, and clean up on all paths.

sections.body: A reliable pattern uses one cleanup label so that every failure path closes what was opened. Because `errno` can be overwritten by later calls, capture it right after the failing call.

subtopics.title: POSIX file descriptors and mmap
subtopics.summary: The unbuffered layer under stdio, used for sockets, pipes, locking and durability.

sections.body: `open(path, flags, mode)` returns a descriptor or -1. `read` and `write` may transfer fewer bytes than requested (short counts), so robust code loops until done and retries on `EINTR`. Flags such as `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, `O_APPEND`, `O_TRUNC`, `O_NONBLOCK` and `O_CLOEXEC` give precise control that `fopen` modes cannot. `mmap` maps a file into memory so the kernel pages data in on demand.

takeaways: A `FILE *` is a buffered stream over a descriptor; always check `fopen` for `NULL` and `fclose` for failure.
Drive read loops by the return value of the read call (`fgets`, `fread`, `fscanf`), never by `while (!feof(fp))`.
`"w"` truncates, `"a"` appends at the end no matter what, `"r+"` edits in place, and C11 `"x"` refuses to overwrite.
`fgetc` returns `int` so that `EOF` stays distinct from the 256 byte values.
`fflush` reaches the kernel, `fsync` reaches the disk; crash safety needs the second.
Binary structs written with `fwrite` are not portable: padding, size and endianness all differ across systems.
Bound every `%s` in `fscanf` and use `fgets` or `getline` for lines to avoid buffer overflows.
